story.html: Onosato was already an Ozeki when the tracker switched on, and the rest of the climb took him less than a year. He won championships in back-to-back tournaments in March and May 2025, then a third in September 2025, and that last one carried him to Yokozuna. His shikona means "great village," handed down the line from Takanosato and Kisenosato, the master who trained him. He fights in a midnight blue mawashi. Reaching the top rank that fast is rare, and his record across the climb is the plain explanation for it.

story.html: When the tracker switched on in March 2025, Aonishiki was a Maegashira 15 at the bottom of the top division; about eighteen months later he had climbed all the way to Ozeki. The Ukrainian came up through Komusubi and Sekiwake and collected three championships on the way: Kyushu 2025 as a Sekiwake, January 2026 on the run that first made him Ozeki, and July 2026, where he added a Technique prize after a slip back to Sekiwake. That July run was the wild one. He fought the whole basho on a bad left toe, took out both reigning Yokozuna on back-to-back days, clinched his Ozeki return, and then won the cup in a three-way playoff, all on the same foot. His shikona reads as "blue brocade," a tip of the cap to his master Aminishiki of the Ajigawa stable, with the blue nodding to the flag he came up under. He has favored a British racing green mawashi and a dark muted blue-grey. To the crew, he's just AO.

mawashi.b: BRITISH RACING GREEN was correct through NAGOYA 2026. He changed belts for Aki 2026. The record was not wrong

layers.text: 26KyD2 (Scorekeeper Eye): NEW ROW. The RIGHT foot and ankle are taped and the LEFT is bare.

NEW ROW, NOT A LAYER, and the test is unambiguous. The carried row is 'Aonishiki - left foot/toe/ankle', which names a side. A right-side observation would make that row lie, so it splits. Same call as the Asakoryu side question at Aki D15, which also split on side, and the opposite of the Abi foot-vs-ankle question, which did not.

THE SIDE SWAP IS THE FINDING. This man's left foot has been the single most-tracked item on the project: four flare calls in fifteen days at Aki, three of them resting on the shikiri squat alone. On Day 1 of Kyushu the left was bare and the flare tag came off. On Day 2 the tape is on the other foot.

THE SQUAT SAYS THE LEFT IS GENUINELY QUIET. Jennie: 'he is balanced on squats'. That is the instrument that has caught the left foot before tape ever did, and it is reading clean. So this is not a case of the left problem migrating or being mis-sided; it reads as a separate right-side issue on a man whose left side is currently behaving.
NATURE IS ACUTE, NOT SUSPECTED CHRONIC, because there is a before and after one day apart: bare on Day 1, taped on Day 2. That is an event, unlike Day 1 census tape which has no known onset.

WATCH: whether this is one day of strapping or the start of something, and whether the left stays quiet while the right is loaded. If the left comes back while the right is taped, the two rows want reading together.

26Aki Preview (0.5, air 09-11): Enters Aki the consensus favorite, presumed fit. [booth]
Booth, likely not close to top form yet, still reeling from the left-foot injury. [booth: Raja]

26AkD1 (Scorekeeper Eye): Left foot and ankle taped. Toe reads RECOVERED - the break now believed healed - but the left ankle is still not looking good. (Jennie)
26AkD3 (Scorekeeper Eye): Got up GINGERLY but there was NO LIMPING. Reads as a knock, not an aggravation. (Jennie)

26AkD9 (Scorekeeper Eye): FLARE. 'A definitely limpling after that victory throw' (Jennie, bout 19 vs Yoshinofuji). Nature tagged Flared. First flare on this row since Nagoya, called on her own marker: limping is what distinguishes an aggravation from a knock.

26AkD10 (Scorekeeper Eye): FLARE HOLDS, from new evidence. 'AO still protecting that left foot on the squats (completely flat footed and weight more on the right side).' The shikiri rather than the bout - a steady-state read of what he trusts the foot to do, with nobody forcing anything.
26AkD12 (Scorekeeper Eye): FLARE TAG DROPPED. CHRONIC STAYS ACTIVE. 'a squat left foot back on toe' (Jennie, bout 19 vs Kinbozan, which he won).

THE PROTECTION IS GONE AND THE SAME MEASUREMENT CAUGHT IT. On D10 the left foot was completely flat with the weight shifted right; on D12 it is back on the toe, which is the normal sonkyo posture. He is loading it again. The flare opened on a limp, held on a guarded squat, and closed on the squat returning to normal - three readings, one of them the thing that closed it.
UNDER THE ACTIVATION RULE a flare tag drops when the flare goes and the chronic underneath does not move. Nature is back to Chronic alone; Status stays Active and always would have.

THE METHOD POINT WORTH KEEPING: the squats turned out to be the better instrument twice. They caught the protection on D10 when the walk-off said nothing, and they caught its absence on D12. A limp is an event; the shikiri is a measurement, repeated four times before every bout in full view.
The booth on this day still had him 'fighting through an aggravated left foot injury', which the eye now outruns.

26AkD14 (Scorekeeper Eye): FLARE REOPENED. 'both go off the dohyo k helps ao off. after bout Ao squat left foot flat again, favoring weight on the right' (Jennie, bout 18 vs Kirishima, an Ozeki showdown he won).

THE SAME MARKER, WORD FOR WORD. Flat left foot, weight on the right. That is the identical state she described on D10, and its absence is what closed the flare on D12. Nature tagged Flared again; Status stays Active, as it has throughout, because a chronic never moves on the flare.

THE MECHANISM IS ON THE RECORD THIS TIME. Both men went off the dohyo, which is a load on that foot and ankle, and Kirishima helped him off. The flare is dated to the day of the fall rather than to a later discovery, which is what the retro-dating rule exists to avoid having to do.

FOUR READINGS, FOUR CALLS, ONE INSTRUMENT. Opened D9 on a limp, held D10 on a flat squat, closed D12 on the foot returning to the toe, reopened D14 on it going flat again. The shikiri has been right every time it has been consulted on this man, and it has now been the sole basis for three of the four calls. It is the best-performing observation method on this project.

AND HE IS IN THE YUSHO RACE ON IT, at 11-3, exactly as he was at Nagoya when he played through to the title on the same foot. The record now holds two tournaments of him competing at the top on a flaring chronic, which is the pattern rather than the exception.

story.html: Kirishima has done the hard thing in sumo, which is fall and climb back. He had been an Ozeki, lost the rank, and opened the crew era down in the maegashira, grinding through the named ranks again and again. The reward came at the March 2026 basho: a championship from Sekiwake, and with it a return to Ozeki. He carries the name of his stablemaster, the former Yokozuna Kirishima, and it means "mist island," which is also a volcanic range in Kyushu. He wrestled his earlier career as Kiribayama. The mawashi is a deep brownish purple.

bio.v: Style (booth): versatility and ring sense, an array of weapons and a sharp feel for where he is on the straw, which lets him stay calm under a forward-moving opponent. Watch item: a habit of backing up and pulling when off balance. [Grand Sumo Live, booth, as of 2026-09-13]
霧島 (Kirishima) = 霧 (mist) + 島 (island) → 'Mist Island' (also the Kirishima volcanic range in Kyushu). Confidence: HIGH. Lineage: inherited from his stablemaster, former yokozuna Kirishima.

story.html:
Fujinokawa is one of the youngest men in the division and he has climbed like it, running up through the ranks with an Outstanding Performance prize at the July 2026 basho as a marker along the way. His shikona means "wisteria river," a name the Isenoumi stable brought back into use, and he fought earlier as Wakaikari. He wears a medium blue mawashi. The booth calls him the Mighty Mite. The crew calls him Bloody Eye.

Aki 2026 is the basho that made the case. In his sanyaku debut he beat all three Ozeki, taking Aonishiki, Kotozakura and then Kirishima on day 12. He also carries a 4-0 record against Yokozuna opponents, which makes him only the fourth man in history to win his first four bouts against them. He gives away size to nearly everyone he meets and wins anyway, on speed and refusal. The booth took to calling him the human highlight reel. He finished 11-4 and took the Fighting Spirit Prize.

He works the tawara. Twice in the closing days of Aki he kept himself in on the straw bales and came back out of it, the second time using the bale as an anchor point to turn the bout around rather than just to survive it. It is the method behind the highlight reel.

layers.text: 26AkD9 (Scorekeeper Eye): RIGHT ELBOW WRAPPED. 'F r elbow wrapped' (Jennie, bout 17 vs Kotozakura, the day's Upper bout of the day, which he won by uwatenage).

FIRST INJURY ITEM OF HIS CAREER ON THIS RECORD. Fujinokawa carried nothing at all through the first eight days of Aki and has no prior row of any kind. He is in his sanyaku debut, on a four-bout winning streak into this bout, and the booth has called him the most exciting man in the building every day this week.

WORTH WATCHING RATHER THAN WORTH WORRYING ABOUT YET: one day of wrapping on a man with no history is the weakest kind of signal. What makes it worth a row is that it is the FIRST thing on a clean record, and the onset date is the whole value if it turns into something.
26KyD1 (Scorekeeper Eye): CLOSED. 'yeah the sleeve is off fujinokawa' (Jennie, 2026-11-13). Tape gone on an acute row, activation rule closes it. Status Dormant.

IT RESOLVED THE WAY THE ROW HOPED IT WOULD. Opened on Aki D9 as the first item ever on a clean record, with the onset date as the whole point. It did not become anything: the wrap lasted the back half of Aki and is gone by the next basho. The row has done its job and the dated onset stays on file in case the elbow reappears.
HE IS OTHERWISE CLEAN ON DAY 1. The only thing Jennie recorded against him was a new mawashi colour.

bio.v:
Style (booth): poise and edge-defense beyond his years. Stays in contention with a resourceful last-moment grip and balance; promoted straight past Komusubi into Sekiwake. [Grand Sumo Live, booth, as of 2026-09-13]

RELENTLESS TO THE END. Murray Johnson's line for him, Aki 2026 Day 6, after Fujinokawa absorbed a leg trip, a second leg trip, an attempted sototmuso and a kubinage from Aonishiki and still won by yorikiri. Jennie: 'F just never gives up... so many techniques.' Filed here as a permanent characterisation on her call, and separately as a Catchphrase Library phrase with a Day 6 Sighting. [booth: Murray, air 2026-09-18]

Does not retreat, by his own account. Interview the same day: 'the last thing I wanted to do was retreat after we grappled with each other.' At 177cm he is the shortest man in the joi and routinely gives away 40 kilos, which is what both his nicknames are getting at from opposite directions.
藤乃川 (Fujinokawa) = 藤 (wisteria) + 乃 (poss.) + 川 (river) → 'Wisteria river.' Confidence: MEDIUM. Lineage: a revived Isenoumi-beya shikona.

story.html: Churanoumi has climbed quietly and steadily into the upper maegashira. His name is the best kind of hometown flag: he is Okinawan, and "chura umi" is the beloved Okinawan phrase for the beautiful sea, so the shikona simply means "beautiful sea." He fought earlier as Kizaki. He wears a purple mawashi.

bio.v: 美ら海 (Churanoumi) = 美ら (chura — 'beautiful' in Okinawan) + 海 (sea) → 'Beautiful sea.' Confidence: HIGH. Context: Okinawan-born; 'chura umi' is the famous Okinawan phrase for the beautiful sea.

story.html:
Asanoyama is a former Ozeki on the way back. The tracker caught him down in juryo in late 2025, and from there he has climbed back up through the division. His shikona reads as "morning mountain," the "asa" marking him as a Takasago man, and he fought earlier as Ishibashi. He wears a deep plum purple mawashi. A former top-ranker rebuilding in real time is one of the more compelling arcs on the board.

He has said how close it came to ending. Before the Aki 2026 basho he told announcer Hiro Morita that after facing so many challenges he once thought about quitting, and that he kept going because he wanted to repay his loyal fans and knew he still had more he wanted to accomplish. Morita shared it on air on day 11, the day Asanoyama beat Kinbozan for his winning record.

layers.text: Kyushu2026D4: He damaged both knees since then, but is now back in the joi ranks. [booth, carrying]

injuries.area: General / stamina (post left-knee ACL comeback); visible tape 26KyD2: left knee, right knee, left ankle, left hand. Right glute still absent since 26AkD14

layers.text: Murray again framed him as working back from injury (comeback context, bout vs Takerufuji). [booth]

26AkD1 (Scorekeeper Eye): LEFT KNEE BANDAGED - the ACL knee. First visible corroboration of the comeback, which until now has only ever been narrated by the booth. Right leg also taped above and below the knee; left hand taped. (Jennie)
26AkD14 (Scorekeeper Eye): RIGHT GLUTE TAPED. New site, never seen on him before. 'A right glute is taped' (Jennie, bout 17 vs Fujinokawa, the Lower BOTD, which he lost as a co-leader at 10-3).

LAYER, NOT A NEW ROW, and the test is what decides it. This row's Area is general and stamina-based; it names no sites, so a taped glute cannot make it lie. The Lisfranc row would have been made to lie, which is why the glute does not go there. Under the new-row-vs-new-layer test a new observation that does not contradict the claim is a layer.

IT ALSO LANDS ON THE GRANULARITY QUESTION JENNIE PARKED. This row has been quietly acting as the catch-all for his visible tape - left knee, right leg, left hand, now the glute - which is exactly the multi-site drift in the register, and opening a thin new row for one day of glute tape is precisely the call she deferred until one full tournament of injury data is in hand. Deliberately not deciding that mid-basho. Flagged for the post-basho remodel as a worked instance.

WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT WRITTEN: any link between the glute and the reconstructed left knee. A glute taping on a man thirteen days into a comeback invites that inference and it is an inference, not an observation. The fact tier gets the tape; nothing gets the chain.

HE IS 13 DAYS INTO A TOURNAMENT at roughly 70% comeback condition, carrying a left knee, a right leg, a left hand, a Lisfranc foot and now a glute. Worth stating plainly because the row's own subject is accumulated load, and this is what that looks like.

NO OBSERVATION, AND THE QUESTION GOES UNANSWERED. The Day 15 sheet asked explicitly whether the glute tape was still there, because one day of tape and a persistent wrap are different signals and the record cannot currently tell them apart. Jennie logged nothing on him at bout 12, so under the carry-forward rule the silence carries and the glute stays on the row as observed.

SO THE ONE-DAY-TAPE QUESTION ENDS THE BASHO OPEN, ON THE CLEANEST TEST CASE IT HAD.  This is not a failure of the pass - a scorekeeper is not obliged to notice an absence, and 'only removals get an explicit note' is the standing rule precisely because noticing every absence is impossible. It is a demonstration of the gap: the one signal the remodel needs to distinguish is the one the current model gives no way to capture, and it slipped on the day it was explicitly being watched for.

FOR THE POST-BASHO REMODEL: if a one-day tape is to become its own acute row, the checklist has to ASK about yesterday's new tape by name rather than relying on a removal being volunteered. That is a checklist-format change, not just a schema change, and it is the practical half of the granularity decision.

HE FINISHED 10-4 after losing bout 12 to Yoshinofuji, which Pass 1 says cost him the Fighting Spirit Prize. Five taped sites, a Lisfranc foot and a reconstructed knee, at roughly 70%, to a double-digit record.
Carried in — left foot (missed 3 days in May).
Still the Lisfranc issue, managing it.
26AkD1 (Scorekeeper Eye): No left-foot tape observed. The knee and the right leg were what showed. Lisfranc not visible this day - absence of tape, not evidence of resolution. (Jennie)
26AkD3 (Scorekeeper Eye): Second look, same picture. Still no left-foot tape; the knee and the right leg are what show. Two of three days now. (Jennie)

RULE SETTLED 2026-09-25 (Jennie): 'it could close a flare up but a chronic by default stays active.' Absent tape does NOT close a chronic, whatever its source. The activation rule closes an ACUTE item and closes a FLARE on a chronic; the chronic itself stays Active.
26AkD4 (Scorekeeper Eye): LEFT FOOT AND ANKLE TAPED. After three days of nothing on it, the Lisfranc is visibly strapped. (Jennie)

THE RULE PAID OFF IMMEDIATELY. Had absent tape been allowed to ease this row on Day 3, Day 4 would have reopened it a day later. What the first three days actually showed was days he chose not to strap it, not a condition going quiet. Status was Active throughout and stays Active. Note for anyone reading the earlier layers: the absence was never evidence, and this is the proof.

26AkD7 (Scorekeeper Eye): LEFT FOOT STILL TAPED. (Jennie) Second observed day running with the Lisfranc strapped, after D4. The on-and-off pattern of D1 through D3 has not come back. Status stays Active.

bio.v:
Signature style: migi-yotsu. Right hand inside under the opponent's left armpit, working to his preferred grip and stance, finishing with yorikiri (frontal force-out).

Comeback: former Ozeki rebuilding after a left-knee ACL layoff; the booth's throughline on him is determination and fighting spirit through the climb back.

Current-form read (Aki 2026): judged around 70 percent of his former self, stamina the lingering drag, not a yusho threat yet, aiming to climb back toward sanyaku and Ozeki.

[Grand Sumo Preview, air 2026-09-11, booth color]
朝乃山 (Asanoyama) = 朝 (morning) + 乃 (poss.) + 山 (mountain) → 'Morning mountain.' Confidence: HIGH. Lineage: Takasago 朝- prefix.

story.html: Ura is the one who never sits still on the banzuke. He bounces from the upper maegashira down into the low teens and back up, and the crowd could not care less about his lack of silverware. What they come for is the way he wins. Ura built his reputation on acrobatic, unorthodox sumo, the kind of bout that ends with an opponent flipped over a hip or marched backward out of the ring by a plan nobody saw coming. The mawashi is cherry blossom pink, which fits him about right. He is one of the tougher outs in the division to prepare for.

layers.text: Kyushu2026D6: Concerned for Ubi, I'm surprised he's continuing to fight. This ankle is so bad he can hardly move... he cannot do anything on that sore ankle. I'm surprised he's keeping going. [booth, carrying]
26AkD1 (Scorekeeper Eye): Both knees in heavy bandage wrapping, not tape. First logged as its own row.

TRUE ONSET PREDATES THIS ROW. Onset Day is set to Aki 2026 Day 1 because that is the first day it was logged, not the first day it existed. Per Jennie: 'Knees are chronic for Ura, for as long as I've been watching he's been the michelin man.' Split out from the 'Ura - general / feet' row on 2026-09-24 because the visible wrapping is on the knees, not the feet, and the two are separate conditions. (Jennie)
Came in with feet problems; struggles to stay fit.

26AkD1 (Scorekeeper Eye): BOTH KNEES in heavy bandage wrapping - 'looks like the Michelin man.' Right hand and wrist taped, left hand taped. No foot tape observed, so the visible problem is NOT where this row says it is. Knees may warrant their own row. (Jennie)
26AkD3 (Scorekeeper Eye): No tape on Ura's feet. Second look, same finding. The knees row (split out separately) is where the visible wrapping actually lives. (Jennie)

RULE SETTLED 2026-09-25 (Jennie): 'it could close a flare up but a chronic by default stays active.' Absent tape does NOT close a chronic. The activation rule closes an ACUTE item and closes a FLARE on a chronic; the chronic itself stays Active. Status stays Active and this row is no longer an open question.
STILL WORTH A LOOK, but as a different question: this row is filed as feet and the visible wrapping is on the knees. That is a row pointed at the wrong body part, not a candidate to close.
RETIRED AS SUPERSEDED (Jennie, 2026-10-07): 'and yeah ura should be all about the chronic knees.'

Ten days of looking produced no foot tape on any day. The condition this row claims has never once been visible, while the knees have been in heavy wrapping every single day. The row is not wrong about Ura being perennially hurt; it is wrong about WHERE, and it has been wrong since Nagoya. 'Ura - both knees (chronic)' carries the real condition.

READ THIS DORMANT CAREFULLY. It does NOT mean the feet got better, and it is not the activation rule firing - a chronic never closes on absence, and that rule stands. It means the FILING is retired. The booth's Nagoya 'came in with feet problems' stays on the record as the claim it always was.

FLAGGED FOR THE POST-BASHO REMODEL: this is now a third distinct meaning of Dormant. (1) an acute whose tape went, (2) a watch row whose condition resolved, (3) a mis-filed row superseded by a better one. Three meanings in one value is a wobble, and the remodel should decide whether superseded wants its own status or whether a relation to the replacing row is enough.

bio.v: 宇良 (Ura) = 宇 (u, eaves/the heavens) + 良 (ra, good/fine) — his real surname, so the 'meaning' is incidental. Confidence: MEDIUM (real-name shikona). Context: famed for acrobatic, unorthodox techniques.

story.html: Takayasu is one of the elder statesmen of the division, a former Ozeki who still trades with the best of them. At the July 2026 basho he took a Fighting Spirit prize, won in a long grind over Asanoyama in the Nagoya heat that, oddly, seemed to ease his chronic bad back. One booth note the crew logged: his mawashi is famously tight, wrapped so hard that opponents cannot get a finger or a nail under it, which is a big part of why nobody can find a grip on him. He fights in a dark blue mawashi. Around the crew he is Hairy, or Papayasu.

layers.text: 26KyD1 (Scorekeeper Eye): New row by Jennie's call, 2026-11-13, kept separate from the existing 'Takayasu — chronic (May layoff)' row.

WHY SEPARATE RATHER THAN AMENDED: the May row is explicitly Unspecified, 11 days out for something never named. There was a precedent for filling an Unspecified row's Area from the Scorekeeper Eye (Takerufuji, 26AkD1), but balls-of-feet tape is common and coupling it to an unknown May layoff would be inventing a link. Jennie chose the new row.
IF THE TWO TURN OUT TO BE THE SAME THING, merge this into the May row rather than the other way round, since that row holds the layoff history.
Aki2026D9: Takayasu landed hard outside the dojo and looks woozy. He tells the yobidashi he is okay. [booth]
26AkD9 (Scorekeeper Eye): CONFIRMED BY THE EYE. 'T fall is slow to get up but says he's ok' (Jennie, bout 16 vs Atamifuji, lost by oshitaoshi).
SECOND OFF-DOHYO LANDING ON THIS CARD IN THREE DAYS, after Hakunofuji on D7. The same watch applies: normal on the card on Day 10 closes this row; absent or passive and it is more than woozy.

THE EVIDENCE HERE IS WEAKER THAN IT LOOKS. 'He tells the yobidashi he is okay' is the man's own word, given seconds after the fall, by a 36-year-old who the booth says makes no excuses. That is the least reliable source available on a head-ish event and it is the only source the booth had.

SECOND TIME THE WATCH-CONDITION PATTERN HAS WORKED IN FOUR DAYS, after Hakunofuji's head row. WHY FRESH MATTERS. The standing rule on cupping is that a fading bruise is a weak signal, because it only tells you the cupping happened a while ago. A FRESH bruise is the opposite: it dates the treatment to within a day or two and means something was being treated right now. That is why this opens a row rather than sitting as colour.
Nature is Suspected chronic rather than Acute for the same reason the back row is: the area is inferred from where the marks are, not from a stated diagnosis.

The booth flagged unspecified 'injury concerns' on him twice this basho, D5 and earlier, and never named anything. Because the row existed, the concussion is dated to DAY 11, attributed to the mechanism that caused it, and tied to the bout - instead of surfacing as a Day 12 withdrawal with no history behind it.

story.html:
Tamawashi is the iron man of the division, and the streak is the whole story: since his 2004 debut he has never missed a bout. Not one, in a sport that breaks people. A Mongolian veteran out of Kataonami, his shikona reads as "jewel eagle," the 玉 prefix being the stable's signature mark. He rose as high as Sekiwake, and when he drops to juryo he climbs straight back out of it, still moving at an age when most of the men judging his bouts are younger than he is. He fights in a dark steel blue mawashi. The booth just calls him the Iron Man.

He is also the oldest man ever to climb back into the top division. He came up from juryo for the Kyushu basho of 2026 and turned 42 in the middle of it, in his 101st tournament in makuuchi.

So the observation belongs here, on the carried ACL, not on a new site.

Nature tagged Worsened. A retweak of a carried structural injury is the condition getting louder, and 'retweaked' is her word. Reversible.

HOW THIS WAS HANDLED, because the handling is the point: a separate left-knee row WAS opened on the first read, precisely because this row names a side and a left knee would have made it lie. That was the new-row-vs-new-layer test working correctly on the information available. Her one-word correction moved the observation here and the stray row was retired as superseded the same session. The test protected the sided claim instead of quietly overwriting it, which is what it is for.
THIS ROW CROSSES THE BASHO BOUNDARY WORSENED, on an ACL carried since May, with no further observation available until Kyushu.

story.html: Oho carries one of the heaviest names in sumo. He is the grandson of the legendary Yokozuna Taiho, whose name meant "great roc," and Oho inherits the roc, so his own reads as "king roc." He has reached Sekiwake and Komusubi more than once. He came up as Naya. He wears a dark purple mawashi. When he is right, the joi is where he belongs.

story.html: Abi is a big pusher-thruster. When his thrusting attack is on it is relentless and he can beat anyone; when it is off the results wander, which is roughly the shape of his banzuke line. His shikona reads loosely as "blaze." He came up as Horikiri. He wears a midnight blue mawashi.

story.html: Asasuiryu made his top-division debut in September 2026 after a run in juryo. A Takasago man, his shikona reads as "morning jade dragon." He came up as Ishizaki.
